analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice awards for pain and suffering, forces insurers to cut doctors' premiums, and publicizes doctor discipline records.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 21, 2005 with three cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees and a Health Subcommittee and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill capped what a patient could recover for pain and suffering from a malpractice lawsuit at $250,000 adjusted for inflation from 1975 — roughly $878,000 for 2005 — while requiring malpractice insurers to pass at least half of their resulting savings to doctors as lower premiums. It also created a public interstate database of doctors' malpractice payouts, discipline, and criminal convictions, set performance standards for state medical boards, funded mediation to resolve claims without lawsuits, gave legal protection to hospitals' internal patient-safety analyses, and explicitly left drug and device makers outside the new limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors gain the most directly: a ceiling on the largest malpractice awards, lower insurance premiums paid partly out of insurer savings, and immunity for good-faith reports about colleagues to state medical boards. Patients also gain practical tools — a public, searchable record of each doctor's malpractice payouts, disciplinary actions, and criminal convictions; state medical boards held to complaint-processing and disclosure standards; and funded mediation as an alternative to court. Doctors benefit from the cap in a way that comes at injured patients' expense; the disclosure and safety provisions benefit patients directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors facing lawsuits; patients researching physicians

how_it_helps.text: Patients could look up any physician's education, specialty, malpractice payouts, hospital discipline, criminal convictions, and state board discipline for the previous 10 years, online or by toll-free phone, through a new interstate database that also accepted and tracked patient complaints [S3].

State medical boards would have to meet voluntary performance standards: process complaints within a set time, let patients track their complaints, keep adequate qualified staff, and publish physician discipline and claims history [S2][S3].

The Attorney General would make grants to states and health care entities for mediation programs, modeled on Rush-Presbyterian-St. Luke's program in Chicago, to resolve malpractice allegations without litigation, with apologies kept confidential [S2][S3].

Health care workers who report safety information in good faith would be protected from retaliation — demotion, bad evaluations, or other adverse employment actions — with civil penalties up to $20,000 per violation against a provider that retaliates [S3].
The damage cap was set far higher than the flat $250,000 caps debated in Congress that year: $250,000 adjusted for inflation from 1975, estimated at about $878,000 for 2005 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The heaviest cost falls on patients most severely injured by malpractice — people whose losses are pain, disfigurement, or the death of a child rather than lost wages — because their compensation is capped even when a jury would award more, and the federal cap overrides state laws that allow larger recoveries. Medical malpractice insurers bear a new obligation to dedicate at least half of their savings from the cap to cutting doctors' premiums, enforced only through their own certifications and reports, with civil penalties up to $11,000 per violation.

drawbacks.text: Capping non-economic damages limits recovery most for the patients hurt worst by negligence — infants injured at birth, the elderly, and people left disabled — whose damages are overwhelmingly pain and suffering rather than lost income [S2][S3].

The federal cap overrides state law from above: states may allow less, but no state may permit a recovery above the federal maximum, so patients in states that rejected caps would still be capped [S3].

Every malpractice complaint would have to carry a certification of merit, and a court 'shall' hold a violating lawyer or party in contempt, award costs and fees, and impose fines — and after repeat violations refer the lawyer to the state bar — raising the risk and cost of pursuing any claim [S3].

Internal hospital analyses of medical errors would become legally privileged and shielded from subpoenas, discovery, and freedom-of-information requests, so the documents most likely to show what went wrong could be kept out of a patient's lawsuit [S3].

The insurance provisions are soft: the rate-increase oversight in Section 401 is only a statement that 'the Congress intends' states to adopt it, enforced by a survey and a report, and the premium-reduction mandate leans on insurers' own estimates of their savings, self-certified to HHS [S3].

Hospitals, doctors, and nurses gain immunity for reporting a physician's competence or conduct to a state medical board unless they knew the information was false, which narrows recourse for a doctor unfairly accused [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a more patient-friendly design than the malpractice caps Congress debated that year: the cap was set around $878,000 after inflation adjustment rather than a flat $250,000, insurers were forced to hand half their savings back as premium cuts, and the bill paired the cap with real transparency — public doctor records, board standards, complaint tracking, and funded mediation. But the people with the most at stake — patients catastrophically injured by negligence — still bore the cost, since their awards would be capped no matter what a jury found, the shield over internal safety analyses would keep key evidence out of court, and the insurance premium mandate rested on insurers' own numbers with modest penalties. A fair reading is that doctors and insurers gained more than patients did, while patients got genuine new tools to check on their doctors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with three cosponsors, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, sent to a Health Subcommittee five days later, and never received a markup, a committee vote, or floor action before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Baird, a Democrat from Washington, introduced the Comprehensive Medical Malpractice Reform Act of 2005 on July 21, 2005, joined by Representatives Moran of Virginia, Ruppersberger of Maryland, and Lipinski of Illinois [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
On August 5, 2005 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill never received a vote in either committee or on the House floor before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Malpractice victims kept uncapped state-law remedies that the bill would have limited, while physicians and malpractice insurers avoided the new public disclosure requirements, board performance standards, and forced premium reductions the bill would have imposed on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Victims kept full remedies; doctors avoided disclosure

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but all four sponsors were Democrats and the bill sat untouched in the Republican-controlled House, which pursued its own malpractice legislation instead.

industries.industry: Physicians and other licensed health care providers
industries.note: The damage cap, mandated premium relief, and immunity for good-faith reports to medical boards all lower doctors' malpractice exposure — a gain that comes directly out of compensation owed to injured patients. In exchange, doctors would have taken on public disclosure of their malpractice payouts, discipline, and criminal convictions.

Capping the largest awards would cut what insurers pay on claims, but the bill forced each insurer to dedicate at least half of those savings to reducing physicians' premiums, backed by self-certification, annual reports, and civil penalties up to $11,000 per violation. The industry's central interest — paying less on claims — runs against injured patients' full recovery.

Capped awards shrink contingency fees, and the certificate-of-merit requirement with mandatory contempt, fee-shifting, fines, and bar referral after repeat violations raises the personal and financial risk of taking malpractice cases. The trial bar's interest in uncapped recoveries runs alongside injured patients'.

The bill would have created a certification system for patient safety organizations and made hospitals' internal error analyses privileged from discovery, encouraging voluntary reporting of safety problems. The shield keeps candid internal analysis flowing but also keeps that evidence away from injured patients in court.

Title V explicitly excludes drug and device makers from the damage cap and mediation programs, leaving their product-liability exposure under state law untouched even as claims against doctors and hospitals are capped. That carve-out keeps unlimited recovery available against them while their co-defendants in care are protected.
